state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you explain why you think changing all values by the same proportion wouldn't affect the range in both scenarios? How does the concept of range relate to the individual values in the data set?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think if you cut all the plants in half, the smallest and largest heights would still be in the same proportion to each other, so the range wouldn't change. But with Katie's example, I'm not really sure why adding \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) would be different. Can you explain how the range works with those changes?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: How do you think adding 3 cm to each plant's height would affect the relative positions of the smallest and largest plants in the data set? Can you think of a specific example where changing all values by the same amount would clearly impact the range?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher fails to correct the student's fundamental misconception that proportional changes don't affect range (which is mathematically incorrect—halving all values halves the range), and the student shows no improvement, ending more confused than at the start.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions and avoids giving direct answers, which aligns with Socratic method, but fails to use counterexamples to expose the student's flawed reasoning about proportional changes affecting range, and doesn't directly address the misconception revealed in Turn 2.
